summary: For ages 9–11, build understanding of the atmosphere along two threads: (1) air is real matter that has weight and exerts pressure in all directions, countering 'air is nothing', and (2) the atmosphere is a thin, layered shell around Earth whose lowest layer, the troposphere, holds almost all weather. Combine a labelled cross-section and zoom-out scale reveal with hands-on air-has-weight and pressure investigations, and name the atmosphere's protective (radiation) and warming roles as distinct from its structure.
misconceptions: Air is 'nothing' / has no weight — air is matter, has weight and exerts real pressure
The atmosphere is enormously thick / space starts just above the clouds — the life-supporting layer is very thin
Weather happens throughout the whole atmosphere — nearly all weather is in the troposphere
The atmosphere and the ozone/greenhouse ideas are the same thing — they are distinct roles of the air
Pressure only exists in tyres/balloons, not in the open air around us

activities.title: Climb-the-layers atmosphere explorer with a scale reveal
steps: Starting at the ground, move upward through a labelled cross-section of the atmosphere, tapping each layer to reveal facts (e.g. tap the troposphere to see that clouds, storms and nearly all weather are packed into it)
Trigger a zoom-out scale reveal that shrinks the whole life-supporting atmosphere to a thin skin hugging the Earth globe, with all weather crammed into the bottom sliver

Open lift-the-flap facts such as 'air has weight' and 'the air around you is pressing on you right now', and a 'where does space really start?' flap showing that air thins gradually with height, that space is commonly said to begin about 100 km up (far above the clouds, which are mostly within roughly the bottom 10–15 km), and that even 100 km is tiny compared with Earth's size
State in your own words where weather happens and how thin the life-supporting layer is compared with Earth's size
activities.insight: The atmosphere is a thin, layered shell compared with Earth's size. Nearly all weather happens in the lowest layer, the troposphere, which is only a paper-thin skin around the globe. The air does not go up forever: it thins with height, and space is commonly said to begin about 100 km up, well above the clouds but still very close compared with Earth's width.

activities.title: Feel that air is real matter: weigh it and watch pressure
steps: Predict whether an inflated ball weighs more, less, or the same as the deflated ball and say why, then weigh both on a sensitive balance to check
Observe (or model) a crush-the-can demonstration and the upturned-glass-of-water-on-card demonstration, describing what the air is doing
Climb through the layers while watching a pressure gauge fall as altitude rises (and, within the troposphere, the temperature drop), and describe how air thins with height
Answer: if air presses on us all the time, why don't we feel squashed? And which direction(s) does air pressure push?
activities.insight: Invisible air is real matter with mass: pumping extra air into a ball makes it measurably heavier, and the whole atmosphere of air above us presses on us as air pressure that acts in all directions, not only downward.

activities.title: Separate the atmosphere's roles and connect it to Earth systems
steps: Match each described job to the air: shielding us from harmful radiation, keeping the planet warm enough for life, and holding our weather
Explain how the atmosphere links to the greenhouse effect and the water cycle so it is seen as an active system, not just 'the sky'
Describe one way the atmosphere interacts with another Earth sphere (geosphere, hydrosphere, or biosphere)
Distinguish the protective/warming roles of the air from its layered physical structure, noting they are different ideas
activities.insight: The atmosphere performs distinct roles — protection from radiation, warming, and carrying weather — and acts as one interacting Earth system rather than a single undifferentiated 'ozone/greenhouse' idea.

activities.title: Reference check: label the layers and locate the weather
steps: Label the layers of the atmosphere from the ground up
Answer a 'where does weather happen?' multiple-choice item and justify the choice
Match each layer to a feature (e.g. weather/clouds to the troposphere)
Explain whether a ball pumped up with extra air weighs more than the same ball deflated, and how you could check on a sensitive balance
activities.insight: Learners can name the layered structure, localise weather to the troposphere, and articulate that air has measurable weight.

activities.title: Ask a pilot or atmospheric scientist (optional extension)
steps: Pose questions to a pilot or atmospheric scientist about how air thins with altitude and why it is clearer above most of the weather
Connect their answers back to the layered cross-section and the pressure gauge
Summarise which layer planes typically fly in and why the air is thinner there
activities.insight: Everyday aviation experience makes thinning air with altitude and the location of weather concrete and relatable.

checkQuestion: We can't see or easily feel the air around us. Does a room full of air weigh anything, or is air weightless? And where does our weather actually happen in relation to the whole atmosphere?
checkAnswer: Air does have weight — a whole atmosphere of it presses on us as air pressure (about 1 kg on every square centimetre). Air isn't 'nothing.' Weather happens in the troposphere, the lowest, thinnest layer of the atmosphere, where almost all the water vapour and clouds are.
